title: Every building modelled so far
premise: Walk every building on Prairie Avenue modelled in detail so far, most detailed first, kept area by area. It grows as buildings are built out.

opening.text: WALK: BUILT SO FAR. The 50 most detailed of the 96 Prairie Avenue buildings modelled past their first rough model, in 1 area. A walk holds 50 stops, so 46 less detailed buildings wait outside it until they gain detail. Most detailed first, one area at a time, so the route does not double back. It is rewritten from the building records whenever one gains detail.

evidence.locator: HABS ILL-1015 data pages 13-15 (PDF pp. 14-16): roofs, walls, courtyard elevation, adjoining-house brick, iron-work, windows, the narrow north windows along 18th Street; p. 9 (PDF p. 10): the courtyard entrance from the alley, the Virginia creeper on the courtyard walls and the Boston ivy on the front; p. 15 (PDF p. 16): the service entrance through the great arch on Eighteenth Street.

evidence.text: In 1910 wreckers destroyed the mansion at 1720 Prairie, the first of many Prairie Avenue homes to be torn down, as the street's residences increasingly gave way to offices, warehouses and factories.
evidence.locator: The essay's closing paragraphs on the street's decline.

evidence.text: 1736 Prairie stood on 1 July 1904, as its structure record carries it.
evidence.reasoning: The draft claims the 1904 target and no more: the 1911 sheet draws the building and the T-1840 census rules it present in 1904 (present_as_mapped). THE HOUSE'S DATE AND ITS MANSARD'S (T-2962): the house was 'completed in 1864' for Granville S. Ingraham (glessner_blog_2020_07_early_history_prairie_iv) — or, as the Prairie library reads an 1875 permit for this lot, built for Gen. Henry Strong in 1875 (T-3037; the structure's `built` carries both) — and that post's author judges the mansard 'may well have been a later addition' to an Italianate house of the Civil War years; nothing read here dates the mansard, and the Keith house at 1900 Prairie had its mansard added in the 1880s (glessner_blog_2014_11_elbridge_keith_house), so a later mansard is the street's own pattern, not a proof for this house. For this phase the question is bounded either way: the c. 1890 photograph (earliest 1885) shows the mansard and the veranda front, and the 1911 sheet draws the mansard's curb and prints the house '3B', so the house as built here stood from at least the late 1880s to 1911. The range keeps to the 1904 target because only the front is seen in c. 1890; the flank's bays are the 1911 sheet's. When the house lost the mansard or was demolished is not read.

evidence.text: Osborn R. Keith Residence, 1808 S. Prairie Avenue: the north wall was retained during demolition in 1968 to preserve the private courtyard of the adjacent Glessner house.
